guests.name: Adam Greuel
guests.dek: Guitar and vocals, Horseshoes & Hand Grenades. A Wisconsin songwriter with a band for every mood, and a fly rod in the truck.
guests.bands: Horseshoes & Hand Grenades. The High Hawks. Rucksack Revolution. Adam Greuel & the Space Burritos. Berens & Greuel. Tuttle, Pool & Greuel
guests.glance: Plays: Guitar, vocals. Home base: Wisconsin. The band met at college in Stevens Point. Telluride: Third place, Telluride Band Contest, 2012, with Horseshoes & Hand Grenades. Off the bandstand: Fly fishing guide. On the show: Season 3, Episode 24
guests.heads: Telluride, twice. On the road with the Dusters. Weekend warriors. A band for every mood. Cosmic Nudge. Guitars and rivers
guests.text: Adam Greuel called in from the road at eight in the morning, the morning after a rain-soaked set at Blue Ox, headed west with a cooler full of Wisconsin cheese for friends in Wyoming. It was the first episode of this show recorded on a weekday, and the first before noon. Telluride, twice Horseshoes & Hand Grenades w Jon Stickley "Darlin' Corey" June 4, 2018 7:29 Adam went to his first Telluride Bluegrass Festival as a fan, at 17 or 18. He had been to smaller festivals in Wisconsin and Wyoming, but never one of the big ones. David Byrne of Talking Heads was on the bill. The whole thing, he says, was formative. A few years later he was back with Horseshoes & Hand Grenades, a string band that formed in 2010 after its five members met at college in Stevens Point, Wisconsin. In 2012 they entered the Telluride Band Contest and took third place. At the time, he says, nearly every well-known progressive bluegrass band had come through that contest. It was the clear path. What he remembers most is what happened away from the contest stage. "I don't know that we made as many fans at Telluride Bluegrass Festival in the band competition as we did picking around the festival." Those fans went home and told their friends about the young band they saw. That, he says, is how things started happening. On the road with the Dusters Tuttle Pool n Greuel "Blackwater Voodoo" 4/30/2021 Nashville TN June 1, 2021 1:01 From about 2012 to 2019, Horseshoes was grinding. They opened for Greensky Bluegrass, The Infamous Stringdusters, the McCourys, Yonder Mountain String Band and Railroad Earth. That is how Trevor first heard them, opening for the Stringdusters. Adam had loved the Stringdusters since early high school. He had their first album, Fork in the Road , and listened to it at his high school job. Mandolinist Jesse Cobb , a founding Stringduster who now plays with The Unfaithful Servants, is a fellow Wisconsinite, which may be how the record found him. Getting to tour with them was an honor. "There's something really cool about people who are more successful and know more and are perhaps more skilled, but they're also very willing to share that with younger folks." Weekend warriors Horseshoes and Hand Grenades "Stay Awhile" February 13, 2018 2:33 Trevor asked why so many bands now tour regionally. Adam gave two answers. For Horseshoes, life changed. He is the only full-time musician in the band now. The others have other jobs, so the band plays more like weekend warriors, and he says that suits them. The bigger picture is harder. He thinks it got trickier to sell tickets after COVID, and cheap hotel rooms are gone, so long tours make less sense than they used to. Mid-size bands and small festivals feel it most. "Buying this ticket in advance, buying a CD. That stuff really matters." A band for every mood Horseshoes and Hand Grenades "Stay Awhile" February 13, 2018 2:49 Adam plays in a lot of bands, and he says he loves them all about equally. The High Hawks is a country rock and roll band with Vince Herman of Leftover Salmon, Tim Carbone of Railroad Earth, and Chad Staehly, Brian Adams and Will Trask. They have two albums, the latest Mother Nature's Show . The name came out of a phone call among the members, and for a while Adam wore little wings on stage. Rucksack Revolution is a duo with Sarah Vos of Dead Horses, in the spirit of Gillian Welch and David Rawlings. Adam Greuel & the Space Burritos is his country rock band, named for his love of the Flying Burrito Brothers and Col. Bruce Hampton's "space is the place." And Berens & Greuel is a comedy duo with Midwestern comedian Charlie Berens, with two albums out. "They're all part of my life, and I really do love 'em all. They kind of scratch different itches." Cosmic Nudge Horseshoes and Hand Grenades "Stay Awhile" February 13, 2018 3:05 The best studio story involves Kyle Tuttle and Jared Pool . During the pandemic, Adam had studio time booked at Pachyderm Studios in Minnesota, and his original plans for it fell through. Instead of canceling, he called Kyle and Jared a day or two before and asked them to fly in. They had no material ready. They taught each other songs, made some charts and recorded until it felt right. Some of the songs had been written earlier, when Adam and Kyle were picking together in Michigan's Upper Peninsula. The record became Cosmic Nudge , released in 2021 as Tuttle, Pool & Greuel. At the time of the interview, the trio had reunion dates on the books in Colorado, and Adam hoped for a second album. Guitars and rivers Adam plays Bourgeois guitars. For about ten years his stage guitar was a Bourgeois Vintage D he named Bender, the guitar of his hardest touring years. When Bender was gone, Bourgeois helped him with a Touchstone Signature. Later a friend found a guitar in Canada two serial numbers away from Bender. Adam has it now. It plays and sounds the same. Losing Bender taught him to hold things a little more loosely. Friendships and love, he says, matter more. Off stage, he fishes. He guides fly fishing trips, and when he tours he looks for a river wherever he lands. "Fly fishing is the way that I balance the chaos of being on the road." Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.

guests.name: Alex Genova
guests.dek: Banjo, Jason Carter Band. Six years with Fireside Collective. A bluegrass degree, a jazz guitar master's, and a teaching job at ETSU.
guests.bands: Jason Carter Band. Fireside Collective. Blackberry Bushes Stringband
guests.glance: Plays: Banjo. Guitar too, with a master's degree in jazz guitar. Home base: East Nashville, Tennessee. Schooling: Berklee College of Music (one year). Bluegrass degree, East Tennessee State University. Master's in jazz guitar, Middle Tennessee State University. Teaches: Banjo, student bands and an online American roots music class at ETSU. On the show: Season 4, Episode 35
guests.heads: Piano, guitar, then the banjo. Berklee, the road, and Johnson City. Six years with Fireside Collective. The call from Jason Carter. Back at ETSU. What's next
guests.text: Alex Genova plays banjo in the band Jason Carter put together after leaving the Del McCoury Band. Before that he spent six years in Fireside Collective, which is where Trevor first heard him. Piano, guitar, then the banjo Alex grew up in Wisconsin, in Waunakee. His grandparents lived next door when he was small, and his grandmother gave him piano lessons from a very young age. It did not stick then. As an adult he has gone back to it and is teaching himself. The first instrument that took hold was a guitar he found in his grandparents' closet. It had belonged to his mother. He took lessons and played electric guitar in school bands and rock bands through middle school. Around the end of middle school he found jam bands: Phish, the Grateful Dead, Béla Fleck and the Flecktones. That led to Yonder Mountain String Band, Railroad Earth and Hot Buttered Rum. At the same time he joined the school orchestra and took violin lessons. His teacher also taught fiddle and burned him CDs of roots music, Crooked Still and Bruce Molsky among them. Fiddle looked hard. Banjo looked closer to what he already knew. "I thought that banjo might be easier to learn for me than fiddle, since I had a guitar background. A little more similar. No bow involved." Berklee, the road, and Johnson City He started banjo in high school and went to Berklee College of Music for a year while he was still a beginner. He learned a lot and met players who are now familiar names, Bronwyn Keith-Hynes and Sierra Hull among them. Around 2010, that was. After Berklee he took time off, played with bands around Wisconsin, and went back to school to start a jazz guitar degree at the University of Wisconsin, Stevens Point. Then a Seattle band, the Blackberry Bushes Stringband, hired him. He left school again and toured with them for close to two years. Next came East Tennessee State University in Johnson City, where he earned a degree in bluegrass. In class he met Joe Cicero, the guitarist in Fireside Collective. Alex had already crossed paths with the band once, on a shared bill in Fort Collins, Colorado, during his Blackberry Bushes days. One summer Joe called. The band was looking for a fifth member and wanted him to come down and play some shows around North Carolina. That was the audition. Six years with Fireside Collective Alex played banjo with the Asheville band from 2017 to October 2023. His last show with them was at CaveFest, at The Caverns in Pelham, Tennessee. Trevor was in the crowd. RockyGrass in Lyons, Colorado, holds a special place. Alex went there for years, first for the band contest and then for the banjo contest, which he won. Later he came back with Fireside Collective as a main stage act, one of the high points of his time in the band. The road had its moments. One night at three in the morning the band pulled into the driveway of a friend who had left a door open for them. It was the wrong house. An angry neighbor in pajamas came out to ask what they were doing. They backed the van out, found the right house next door, and left their host a pile of CDs, merch and a poster by way of apology. Another time a slow leak and a snowstorm nearly cost Alex and Joe Cicero a flight out of Denver. They made it, on a nearly flat tire. After Fireside, Alex finished what he had started almost ten years earlier. He earned a master's degree in jazz guitar at Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro. The call from Jason Carter In the summer of 2025, Bronwyn Keith-Hynes asked him to fill in on some dates with her new solo band. Jason Carter called shortly after. Jason had left the Del McCoury Band and the Travelin' McCourys and was building his own group, and he did not have a banjo player yet. Alex has played with him ever since. It is now his full-time gig. The band is new enough that it has not recorded together yet, though Alex expects that to change. What he likes most so far is the company. Jason came up among the first generation of bluegrass players, and he has stories about all of them. "Him and Bronwyn both are great band leaders, and make sure everybody's as comfortable as possible when we're spending that much time on the road." At some of Jason's Nashville residency shows, Michael Cleveland sat in for the second set. Alex calls it a pinch-me moment and admits he still watches the videos. "Playing banjo behind Jason and Michael Cleveland twin fiddling, that's like a dream come true for any banjo player." Another highlight: a run of shows with Bryan McDowell, Jacob Jolliff, Mark Schatz and Jake Stargel, all players he calls heroes. He has not played the Ryman or the Grand Ole Opry yet. He would like to. Back at ETSU Alex lives in East Nashville and drives to Johnson City once a week to teach at ETSU. He gives one-on-one banjo lessons, leads two student bands that change from semester to semester, and teaches an online American roots music class that he especially enjoys. He has also worked the school's summer bluegrass camp. What's next For years he has talked about making his own album. He has a stack of instrumental tunes and is working on arrangements. The open questions are all his own: all instrumental or some vocals, hired singers or his own voice. "I'm nitpicky about it, and can never make up my mind on exactly how I want it to sound."

guests.name: Anj Way
guests.dek: Artist manager and festival marketer with Omni Arts Group. Books First City Music Festival. Started out on a Yonder Mountain String Band street team.
guests.bands: Artist management, festival marketing and booking, social media, tour and album-release planning. Omni Arts Group
guests.glance: Festivals: First City Music Festival, Vincennes, Indiana (co-books it). Folky Fish Fest, St. James, Missouri. Roster: Omni Arts Group artists include Kyle Tuttle, Ettore Buzzini, Gia Welch, The Grateful String Band and Alex Thoele. Got started: Running a street team for Yonder Mountain String Band. On the show: Season 4, Episode 37
guests.heads: A fan first. Going full time. Two festivals, one family. What a manager does. The new kid on the roster. How fans can help
guests.text: Most guests on this show play an instrument. Anj Way works the other side of the stage: the calendars, the posters, the social feeds and the phone calls that get a band from one town to the next. A fan first Anj's first big festival was Bonnaroo. That was where she first heard Yonder Mountain String Band, and she was hooked. She started seeing them all the time, 20 or more shows a year. She got close to the band and started running their street team, recruiting fans in different cities to spread the word. When Yonder brought in a new marketing person who did not know the band well, Anj stepped in to help. From there she made more connections, moved into booking, and then into management. "I never went to school for any of it. I just learned all of it as I got into it. Some things can't be taught. But I'm still learning every day, that is for sure." She is quick to credit that community. Without Yonder, she says, she would not have any of the jobs she has or know any of the people she knows. Going full time For years she worked a day job and did music at night. Around 2018, Omni Arts Group offered her a way to do music full time. It started small and grew from there. She is still grateful for that chance. Then came 2020. Anj had been booking a festival at Terrapin Hill Farm in Kentucky, her first chance to book a whole festival, with The Infamous Stringdusters, Horseshoes & Hand Grenades and Old Salt Union on the bill. It never happened. She kept working anyway, moving her bands' promotion online and helping with small outdoor gatherings in Kentucky. Two festivals, one family Folky Fish Fest takes place at Maramec Spring Park in St. James, Missouri, about an hour and a half from St. Louis. Anj says a lot of its people come from the John Hartford festival world, a festival she also worked, and they are carrying on that family feel and the picking. Her favorite part is the kids jam camp. Young players learn from visiting musicians, then get to perform, including the festival's first set. First City Music Festival in Vincennes, Indiana is a nonprofit run by a board and a committee. Anj came in around 2022 doing only marketing, a couple of months before the fest. Now she books it with co-founder Jeff Deckard. She never knew if she would get to book a festival again after Terrapin Hill, so that means a lot to her. She likes that First City has no overlapping sets, so fans never have to choose. And she still talks about the year a hurricane's leftover weather rolled through during the festival. The crew played through the rain the whole weekend, pretty much on time. "Anybody that was there, you ask them, we're like, 'Man, if we can get through that, we can literally get through anything.'" What a manager does Anj does less booking these days. Management, as she describes it, means working with booking agents to route tours, advancing shows, building timelines for album releases, and handling PR and social media. The work does not stop at five. She runs many social media pages, so a weekend at a festival means scheduling posts ahead for the days she is away. Her favorite part is the marketing: finding the moments that make someone wish they had been there. "It's finding the best moments. Of course the best jams on stage, but the kids blowing bubbles, the people hugging, and just the energy, and being able to portray that into social media." Omni is reshaping itself as a boutique, meeting bands where they are. Some need a full-time manager. Some just need help promoting a tour or planning an album release. The plan is to connect artists with the agents, photographers and production people Omni already knows. Omni has added a partner, and they are adding artists. She also chooses her clients now. Early on she worked with bands that were not her style. "I'm at the point in my career now that if I don't enjoy it or I don't really believe in it, it's not something that I'm gonna put my energy into." The new kid on the roster One artist she is excited about is Ettore Buzzini, an 18-year-old banjo player who was finishing high school when they talked. Her Omni colleague met him at IBMA, and Anj started working with him at the start of 2026. She had not seen him play in person until the Durango Bluegrass Meltdown that March. Her verdict: he might look 18, but he does not play like it. How fans can help Trevor asked about band riders, and Anj had stories: pages and pages of requests, very specific kinds of peanut butter and jelly, and one band that slipped a request for a particular DVD into its rider to see if anyone was reading. Her serious advice is for fans. Buy pre-sale tickets. Take a friend. Buy merch, which she says gets bands from one place to another. Check out the vendors at festivals. And spread the love beyond the biggest names. "Go check out a new band, or go check out a band that's not playing stadiums. It goes a long way."

guests.name: Cory Walker
guests.dek: Banjo, East Nash Grass. A Florida kid raised on newgrass records who named the band and helped build it from a Monday-night bar gig.
guests.bands: East Nash Grass. Suwannee Mountain Boys. Section House. Earlier: Sierra Hull and Highway 111, The Bluegrass Parlor Band, The Dillards, Ricky Skaggs and Kentucky Thunder, Mountain Heart
guests.glance: Plays: Banjo, plus guitar and resonator guitar. Home base: Nashville, Tennessee. Grew up in Lithia, Florida, near Tampa. Honors: IBMA Momentum Award, Instrumentalist of the Year, 2014. IBMA New Artist of the Year with East Nash Grass, 2024. Solo record: School Project (Mountain Fever Records, 2023). On the show: Season 4, Episode 40
guests.heads: A family band from central Florida. Playing with his heroes. East Nash Grass. Earl's guitar at the Ryman. Side projects
guests.text: Trevor called this the most anticipated episode he has ever had. It took about a year to line up. A family band from central Florida "Starlet Iris" East Nash Grass March 16, 2026 0:38 Cory Walker grew up in a house full of pickers. His father plays banjo, and both of Cory's younger brothers play too. The records came first. Before he could talk, he was hearing the New Grass Revival, Muleskinner, Tony Rice, John Hartford, Norman Blake and Peter Rowan, along with plenty of Earl Scruggs and Bill Monroe. At seven he started lessons at the Bluegrass Parlor, a music store in Temple Terrace, near Tampa. By 11 he was the banjo player in the store's band, The Bluegrass Parlor Band, with his brothers on mandolin and guitar. He also studied guitar and a bit of music theory, the part that showed him how music works when you open it up and look inside. Florida, he points out, has a real bluegrass scene, from Lakeland on up to the Georgia line. Trips to IBMA and the Smithville Fiddlers' Jamboree widened his circle. Around 13 or 14, he noticed that most of his friends were musicians, and it hit him that he could just do this for a living. "It's not really helpful to be competitive against others. So it's really a competition with yourself." Playing with his heroes At Smithville, around age 11, he first heard a young Sierra Hull warming up backstage and could not believe anyone that young sounded that good. He later joined her band, Sierra Hull and Highway 111, as a teenager. She would fly him in on weekends. He played on her 2008 Rounder album Secrets , which also features Tony Rice. He earned a business degree at Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro, gigging the whole way. After college he moved to Nashville and worked as a sideman with Nashville Brigade and Mountain Heart, among others. One Mountain Heart show featured Tony Rice. Standing on stage with Rice, Cory says, was one of the coolest things ever. "There's something he does that makes the music dance on its own. It breathes life into everything." The other story that holds up next to that one came earlier. At about 14, Cory was one of a group of young players on an ABC television special that ended with them on stage with Earl Scruggs and Ricky Skaggs at the Tennessee Titans' stadium. The best part happened backstage, where Earl and Cory played together, just the two of them, for about an hour. Cory remembers him as generous with his time. East Nash Grass Cory Walker Banjo Maestro of East Nash Grass July 29, 2026 6:45 After years as a sideman, East Nash Grass is the first band where Cory has ownership. He likes that everybody in the band has a veto, and that the songs are ones they all believe in. He named it, too. He had been booking gigs around town with whoever was free, including a regular spot at Arrington Vineyards, and needed a name. It was East Nashville bluegrass, so it became East Nash Grass. From there the band grew out of a long Monday-night residency at Dee's Country Cocktail Lounge in Madison, just outside Nashville. The moment it turned into a real band came in 2020, a few days into recording their first album at guitarist Jake Stargel's home studio. Cory remembers thinking that they could do this, as its own thing. The self-titled record came out in 2021. "There's a greater reward to building something yourself." Last Chance to Win followed in 2023, recorded at the Tractor Shed in Goodlettsville, a studio Mark Howard built in a shed behind Grandpa Jones's old home. On Harry Clark's "Scarlet Iris," the banjo has a grittier sound. That is a low-tuned banjo with heavier strings, and it belonged to John Hartford. It was sitting in the studio closet when Cory said he wished he had one. "It colors the songs in a special way. It changes what comes out of you." East Nash Grass won IBMA New Artist of the Year in 2024. All God's Children came out on Mountain Fever Records in 2025 and picked up an IBMA Album of the Year nomination in 2026, along with nods for Entertainer and Instrumental Group of the Year. In spring 2026, Frank Rische took over guitar from founding member James Kee. Why has the East Nash lamb never grown into a sheep? Because the band is young and helpless, Cory says, and needs nurturing from the fans. Earl's guitar at the Ryman In July 2025, East Nash Grass played Bluegrass Nights at the Ryman Auditorium. Cory set down the banjo and played Earl Scruggs's 1957 guitar on "Let the Church Roll On." When he heard that the guitar had not been on the Ryman stage since Earl played it, the nerves showed up. He tries to keep that weight out of the way. The best music, he says, comes when he stops watching himself play. "If you want it to sound great, you have to, as best as you can, dissolve into it, to where you can't remember what happened after you get done with the song." Side projects With his brothers and friends including Christian Ward, Cory plays in the Suwannee Mountain Boys. Their short December 2025 run took them to the Basement East in Nashville, Intuition Ale Works in Jacksonville and Cage Brewing in St. Petersburg. He also plays banjo in Section House, an instrumental band with Aaron Ramsey, Bryan McDowell, Jake Stargel and Jeff Partin. He and Harry Clark have recorded a songwriters' project with Christian Ward. His stage banter with Harry Clark is real, he says. They are friends, and they talk to each other on stage the way friends do. Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.

guests.name: Jared Pool
guests.dek: Mandolin. About ten years with Larry Keel, a lifetime at Virginia fiddlers' conventions, and still a grasser.
guests.bands: Larry Keel Experience. Electric Larry Land. Tuttle, Pool & Greuel. Central Virginia Bluegrass Destroyers. Earlier: The Whiskey Rebellion
guests.glance: Plays: Mandolin, guitar, and sings. Home base: Charlottesville, Virginia. Grew up in the Tidewater area. Lived in Richmond from 2009. Record: Cosmic Nudge , Tuttle, Pool & Greuel (2021), cut in two days at Pachyderm Studios in Minnesota. Training: Degree in jazz studies, Christopher Newport University. On the show: Season 4, Episode 36
guests.heads: Grunge first, then Galax. Ten years with Larry Keel. Tuttle, Pool & Greuel. Singing with Peter Rowan. Wednesdays in Charlottesville
guests.text: Trevor had been trying to get Jared on the show for a long time. It was worth the wait. Grunge first, then Galax Jared came to guitar through Green Day, Nirvana and Soundgarden. When his parents finally bought him a guitar, he signed up for a Saturday beginners' class through school. The teacher turned out to be a fine bluegrass player. Jared stayed on as his student, learned fiddle tunes, and at about 12 went with his teacher and his dad to the Old Fiddler's Convention in Galax. By 14 or 15 he was a Galax regular, running into Danny Knicely, Nate Leath, Rex McGee and Larry Keel. Festivals had been part of his childhood in the Tidewater area. He later earned a degree in jazz studies at Christopher Newport University. The mandolin came by accident. In college, a Richmond band called The Whiskey Rebellion needed a mandolin player at the Maury River Fiddlers' Convention in Buena Vista, Virginia. Jared did the best he could and kept going. He moved to Richmond in 2009 to play with them. Ten years with Larry Keel In 2016 Jared took the mandolin chair in the Larry Keel Experience, with Larry on guitar and Jenny Keel on bass. He stayed about ten years, playing in Larry's side projects too. He still plays Electric Larry Land dates when they come up. The road brought a steady run of pinch-me moments. After the passing of Jeff Austin, the Larry Keel Experience helped carry on the Grateful Ball with the Travelin' McCourys. At Grey Fox, in front of the big screens, Ronnie McCoury leaned over during "Friend of the Devil" and said, "Jared, just play a little Friend of the Devil with me." The two of them played the mandolin intro together. "Just to know so many of the people I consider heroes on the scene, and they knew who I was." He has played with Sam Bush, Tyler Childers, the Travelin' McCourys and Steve Earle, and recorded with Rob Ickes, Joan Osborne, Sherman Holmes and the Legendary Ingramettes. Tuttle, Pool & Greuel At the Aiken Bluegrass Festival, organizers liked to throw players together in new combinations. One of those sets put Jared with banjo player Kyle Tuttle and guitarist Adam Greuel , and the three hit it off. In early 2021, Adam had studio time at Pachyderm Studios in Cannon Falls, Minnesota, the room where Nirvana made In Utero . The call came with only a few days' notice. The trio flew north in the Minnesota winter and cut Cosmic Nudge in two days, playing some of the songs together for the first time. For one Halloween show they dressed as dogs in knights' helmets. Three Dog Night. Of course they played "Joy to the World." He would like to do it again. They have talked about it, and as he puts it, they are all keeping the same names, so they can always rely on that. Singing with Peter Rowan Jared had backed Peter Rowan a few times with Larry. About a year before the interview, he got a night in the Outer Banks of North Carolina where he and his friends were Rowan's band for the second half of the show. Rowan asked him to sing "In the Pines," then took the tenor himself and left Jared the lead. Jared remembered every verse. They went on to "Walls of Time" and "Midnight Moonlight," then talked for hours after the show. "He doesn't even really walk, he just floats. It's like a plume of smoke, and it's Peter." His favorite place to play was the Watermelon Park Festival in Berryville, Virginia, on grounds where Bill Monroe and Patsy Cline once played, with the Shenandoah River bending around the site. The festival has since moved. "You could feel the sacred energy there." Wednesdays in Charlottesville Jared stepped back from full-time road life and now lives in Charlottesville. He plays a Wednesday night gig with the Central Virginia Bluegrass Destroyers, a rotating crew that includes Jay Starling of Leftover Salmon. The band is booked for the 2026 Richmond Folk Festival. "If it's everyone, it's awesome. If it's half the band, it's awesome too." The gig keeps him a grasser. Last winter he led the trios that played there, his first real turn as a bandleader. He is thinking about a record of his own, with most of the Destroyers as the band. Mostly he wants to keep playing. "Just trying to play and just trying to bring people happiness and joy in these troubled times."

guests.name: Jesse Cobb
guests.dek: Mandolin, The Unfaithful Servants. Founding member of the Infamous Stringdusters. Raised on fiddle tunes in the Wisconsin woods.
guests.bands: The Unfaithful Servants. The Infamous Stringdusters. The Cobb Brothers
guests.glance: Plays: Mandolin, plus some electric guitar on his own records. Home base: Victoria, British Columbia, on Vancouver Island. Grew up: Dairyland, Wisconsin. Records: Solitude and Another Road (2016), solo. Fallen Angel (2025), with The Unfaithful Servants. On the show: Season 3, Episodes 29 and 30
guests.heads: Tunes by the wood stove. The Cobb Brothers. First week in Nashville. The Stringdusters years. Solitude, then Another Road. The Unfaithful Servants
guests.text: Trevor has been a Jesse Cobb fan since 2008. This two-part conversation was recorded right after IBMA 2025, Jesse's first World of Bluegrass since 2008. Tunes by the wood stove Jesse Cobb Magic #9 January 15, 2015 0:25 Jesse grew up on an 80-acre subsistence farm near Dairyland, Wisconsin. For much of his early childhood the house had no power and no TV. The family kept chickens and a milk cow and made maple syrup. At night the entertainment was a book read aloud, or music. His father played guitar and banjo. His oldest brother, Jed, took up clawhammer banjo, and his brother Shad took up fiddle. Jesse started on guitar, until an older brother claimed it. The only instrument left lying around was a mandolin. "I think my dad showed me three chords, and then I just started banging along with fiddle tunes. And I'd eventually just pick out the melody." Later, when the house had power, the brothers borrowed records from the library in Duluth and Superior, slowed them to half speed and learned them by ear. There was no one nearby who played bluegrass. The Grand Ole Opry on the radio filled the gap. The Cobb Brothers As kids the brothers played festivals around Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Ohio as the Cobb Brothers. They made three recordings for Vetco Records in Cincinnati when Jesse was about 12 or 13. He still has the cassettes. Jon Weisberger, a past guest on this show, has long pushed for them to be reissued. When Jed turned 18 and left the band, the younger brothers followed him into the logging woods. Jesse spent the next years working with his hands: logging, busking on the West Coast with his brothers, helping a family friend train sled dogs in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, and three and a half years repairing railroad bridges from Florida to Oregon. In 1999 he and Jed quit their jobs and drove a two-wheel-drive Ford pickup to Alaska in five days. He barely touched the mandolin in those years. By his mid-twenties he was set on joining the military. His father and brothers talked him into giving music one more try instead. First week in Nashville Blackrock Infamous Stringdusters 11/20/10 Variety Playhouse November 22, 2010 2:25 Jesse moved to Nashville around 2000, where Shad was already part of the scene. At his first jam, Mac Wiseman was holding court and Del McCoury was in the room. A guitar player at that jam asked him to join a two-week tour of Canada. He had a gig in his first week. He had some catching up to do. Traditional bluegrass was never his first love. "I was a New Grass Revival guy. That was my whole thing. Sam Bush." One connection led to the next. He played for a couple of years with Ronnie Bowman, where he got to know Andy Hall and Jeremy Garrett. The Stringdusters years Jesse was the founding mandolin player in the Infamous Stringdusters. The band showcased at IBMA in Nashville in 2005 or 2006, as he remembers it, with a five-song EP and every showcase slot they could find. They left with offers from labels and booking agents. In 2007 their debut, Fork in the Road , came out on Sugar Hill, and the band won three IBMA awards that fall, including Emerging Artist of the Year. He played with the band until 2011. At IBMA 2025 in Chattanooga, he jammed with some of his old bandmates for the first time in years. Solitude, then Another Road After a move to Welland, Ontario, Jesse fell in with Mark Lalama, a Toronto piano player and producer with a home studio. He started sitting in on Mark's local gigs, mandolin next to electric piano and bass. When Jesse said he wanted to make a record, Mark asked him why. Then Mark answered for him: you make an album because you have to. "It's in you, and you've gotta make it." Solitude came out of three improvised, mostly live sessions. The title fit. There were maybe two other mandolin players in town. Another Road followed in 2016, recorded in four days with Ontario session players who did not play bluegrass. The songs took a left turn, and Jesse picked up an electric guitar on some of them. The Unfaithful Servants Back in Victoria, Jesse went to a local musicians' jam at the Duke Saloon. On a break, a stranger sat down beside him. "Hey, you look like you could use a friend." That was Dylan Stone, a songwriter deep in the Victoria scene. They started playing together, and Dylan hired Jesse for a session on his songs. Dylan called the record Dylan Stone and the Unfaithful Servants , a band name he had long wanted, taken from a song by The Band. The group grew from there. Their self-titled debut earned a Canadian Folk Music Awards nomination for New Group of the Year. The pandemic stopped their momentum. The band came back with Quin Etheridge-Pedden on fiddle and Mark Johnson on bass. Their second album, Fallen Angel , produced by Adrian Dolan, came out October 17, 2025. The band made its U.S. debut as an official showcase act at IBMA in Chattanooga, then toured Canada with Shari Ulrich. Coming back to IBMA after so long, Jesse found the same welcome he remembered. "It's just like this big family. No matter how outside you are of the family, you're still welcomed back in." Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.

guests.name: John Boulware
guests.dek: Mandolin, Randy Steele and the High Cold Wind. Fiddle for most of his life. Chattanooga's hired gun.
guests.bands: Randy Steele and the High Cold Wind. Slim Pickins. The Good Old Boys
guests.glance: Plays: Fiddle, mandolin, guitar, bass, and the occasional odd thing. Home base: Chattanooga, Tennessee. Titles: Tennessee State Fiddle Champion, 2006. Alabama State Mandolin Champion, 2013. Four-time fiddle winner at Uncle Dave Macon Days. Telluride: Second place, Telluride Band Contest, 2026, with the High Cold Wind. On the show: Season 4, Episodes 34 and 39
guests.heads: Guitar first, then the fiddle. Playing the contest game. From fiddle to mandolin. Telluride, 2026. The hired gun. Off the bandstand
guests.text: If you have listened to this podcast, you have already heard John Boulware. He wrote the intro music and played fiddle on it, a Slim Pickins tune. The outro is his fiddle too. Guitar first, then the fiddle "Adam and Rose" Randy Steele and The High Cold Wind June 24, 2026 1:46 John grew up in Kimball, Tennessee. At a Boy Scout campout he watched a man play "Smoke on the Water" on a guitar and decided it was the coolest thing he had ever seen. Until then, music was something that came out of the radio. His mother had the country station on, his father had classic rock. He got a guitar for his eleventh birthday. His parents lasted a few weeks of TV jingles picked out by ear, then signed him up for lessons at Opera House Music in South Pittsburg. The teacher who happened to be there was a young Cody Kilby, who showed him a Dylan tune, a Hendrix tune and then "St. Anne's Reel." That was the one. A few months later Kilby left to go on the road with Ricky Skaggs. The fiddle came next. It ran in the family: his grandfather played in a square dance band in Chester, South Carolina, and John still has his fiddle and the amplifier he ran it through. John started lessons with Bob Townsend, and by 12 he had taken Townsend's place in The Good Old Boys, a band on Monteagle Mountain. He stayed about six years. "I got along with everyone, but I didn't really have any good friends that I hung out with, because all of my good friends were in their 70s playing bluegrass at the pickings on the weekends." Playing the contest game At a small festival in Lynchburg, John entered a fiddle contest on a whim and came third. One of the judges was Jim Wood, who called the Boulware house for weeks until his parents agreed to lessons. They drove an hour and a half each way, every week. John credits Wood with most of what he knows about music. What followed was a teenage contest career: the 2006 Tennessee State Fiddle Championship, four fiddle wins at Uncle Dave Macon Days, and in 2013, on a whim again, the Alabama State Mandolin Championship. His secret, as he tells it, was knowing what the judges were listening for. Clean and in the groove beats fast. "Fiddle competitions, when I was growing up, it was really more like a kind of reunion or a gathering that just happened to have a competition going on." The best part was never the stage. It was jamming in the hallway with the people about to compete against him. From fiddle to mandolin John moved to Chattanooga for college at UTC around 2006. The members of Slim Pickins found him teaching at a music store, and he played fiddle with them for years. When several of them formed Randy Steele and the High Cold Wind in 2022, the band needed a mandolin. John filled in, the sound worked, and he stayed. Randy Steele plays banjo and writes the songs, Brad Clark plays guitar, and Justin Hupp plays bass. "The fiddle is my love. It is my first instrument. It is the language that I speak the most fluently." Telluride, 2026 Nick Lutsko & The $100k Band w Randy Steele w John Boulware “Fall Time In Tennessee” August 17, 2024 0:51 The High Cold Wind drove 1,600 miles to the Telluride Band Contest, Randy at the wheel the whole way. It was John's first time west of Texas. On the way up a 200-foot walk at the Continental Divide, he found out what 40 percent less oxygen feels like. They drew the first slot, the one every band dreads. John did not mind. Order does not change the job. They made the final four and played the main stage, finishing second to the Litch Brothers of Orcas Island, Washington. "It would not have been as much fun if we went up there and killed it and did a great job, and the other bands were just kind of okay." The hired gun John calls himself a mercenary. Most of his shows are with Randy Steele now, but he plays everything: bluegrass, old time, Celtic, swing, rock. He has toured Belgium, France, Ireland, Northern Ireland and Holland, soloed twice with the Murfreesboro Philharmonic, helped arrange the music for a production of Dark of the Moon at the University of the South, and played the Chattanooga Ballet's bluegrass production with the High Cold Wind, where every tune had to match the recording the dancers learned it from, measure for measure. He plays in the house band for the dance categories at the Smithville Fiddlers' Jamboree. He has turned down road gigs, deliberately, to keep room for the strange and interesting ones. "I want to leave room for the things that are interesting." He teaches full time, and has for more than 15 years: fiddle, guitar, mandolin, and one dobro student. Off the bandstand He does not play banjo on purpose. Getting good would take the mystery out of it, the same reason he will not learn drums. He loves air drums too much. He is a hand-tool woodworker, currently building his own kitchen cabinets far more precisely than any kitchen requires. He holds a black belt in Kenpo and a shodan in Iaido. His house-on-fire instruments: a French violin from 1781, a Red Diamond mandolin by Don MacRostie, and a small-bodied guitar by Chris Bozung. Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.

guests.name: Ken White
guests.dek: Former executive director of the International Bluegrass Music Association. Led World of Bluegrass to Chattanooga in 2025. Banjo champion at 14, guitar sideman after that.
guests.bands: Executive Director, IBMA, October 2023 to June 2026. Lifetime IBMA member. New Tradition. Sideman work across bluegrass and Americana
guests.glance: Grew up: Louisville, Kentucky. Plays: Guitar, banjo, mandolin. Titles: Kentucky State Banjo Champion at 14. Stages: Grand Ole Opry, Telluride Bluegrass Festival, RockyGrass, Walnut Valley Festival. On the show: Season 3, Episode 23
guests.heads: A banjo for Christmas. The sideman years. A hillbilly musician who reads. Bringing World of Bluegrass to Chattanooga. Advice for new pickers. After IBMA
guests.text: Ken White sat down with Trevor in August 2025, a month before World of Bluegrass came to Chattanooga for the first time. A banjo for Christmas Randy Steele and The High Cold Wind w Ken White "Say Won’t You Be Mine" July 30, 2024 1:14 Ken got a banjo for Christmas when he was 12 and grew up playing bluegrass in Louisville, Kentucky. Two years later he won the Kentucky State Banjo Championship. He does not usually lead with that. He went to the first few IBMA events in Owensboro, and to the ones in Louisville after the move. The banjo came first, but the guitar is what spoke to him. Tony Rice was his hero, and Rice's work with David Grisman led him into jazz, from Grisman to Miles Davis and beyond. He studied guitar at the University of Louisville with the jazz guitarist Jimmy Raney. "Jazz appeals to my intellect, but bluegrass is my heart." The sideman years In his twenties and early thirties Ken played music for a living. For about five years he played guitar in New Tradition, a Nashville band whose leaders included Danny Roberts. They played up to 200 dates a year. He also played with fiddlers Vassar Clements and Deanie Richardson of Sister Sadie, and on stages from the Grand Ole Opry to Telluride and RockyGrass. In Nashville he spent late nights at the Station Inn, helping restock the bar for free nachos and pizza. Life on the road taught him how to pick a gig. "There are three reasons to take a gig. It either has to be good music, good people, or good money. If you've got two of those, it's a great gig. If you have all three, that's the gig I want to do the rest of my life." A hillbilly musician who reads Music school taught Ken to read notation, and that opened doors most pickers never see. He played with the Louisville Mandolin Orchestra, the Nashville Mandolin Ensemble and the Wichita Symphony Orchestra, and he calls sitting on mandolin in the middle of an 80-piece orchestra a once in a lifetime thing. He once played guitar onstage in an opera, in period costume, while the lead soprano sang an aria. He played banjo in a performance of the original jazz band orchestration of George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue . Ken never quit playing, even after he stopped calling himself a professional. In 2002 he co-founded Howerton+White, a marketing agency. He also served as president of the Wichita Jazz Festival. He says learning to improvise in a small group shaped how he works in business, too: supporting other people and keeping the big picture in view. Bringing World of Bluegrass to Chattanooga Ken started at IBMA on October 2, 2023, chosen from more than 70 applicants. He called it a full circle moment. His first World of Bluegrass as director was the last one in Raleigh, the event's home for 12 years. His second was the move. In September 2025, IBMA held World of Bluegrass in Chattanooga for the first time, the organization's 40th year. The business conference ran at the Chattanooga Convention Center. The Bluegrass Ramble put 30 bands in five walkable downtown venues. The closing festival, IBMA Bluegrass Live!, built a multi-stage site across Miller Park, Miller Plaza and Patten Square instead of the riverfront, to keep everything close to the hotels and the Ramble. The staff behind all of it numbered seven, backed by local partners and volunteers. The 2025 Bluegrass Music Awards were held September 18 at Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Auditorium. That year's Hall of Fame class was Hot Rize, the Bluegrass Cardinals and Arnold Shultz. Ken called electing Hall of Famers one of the best parts of the job, a chance to meet the heroes he had when he was learning to play. "If you're throwing the party, you don't really get to enjoy the party." Advice for new pickers Ken's advice for new players is simple. Have fun, whatever your level, and find other people to play with. Ken planned to stop by Randy Steele's Tuesday jam the next time he was in town. "I always tell people, as soon as they learn those first three chords, you just need to get out and play with somebody else, and that will teach you a lot." After IBMA Ken stepped down as executive director in June 2026. In his farewell statement he said he was proudest of the team he built, and that he would remain a lifetime IBMA member, "singing the tenor part and picking an old Martin forevermore." World of Bluegrass returns to Chattanooga October 20 to 24, 2026. Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.

guests.name: Kris Howland
guests.dek: Founder of Heady Wax Fiends. A vinyl record club, a Facebook group and a small label built on one rule: love what you love.
guests.bands: Founder, curator and chief listener at Heady Wax Fiends Record Club
guests.glance: Home base: Denver area, Colorado. Grew up: Outside Toledo, Ohio. The club: A monthly vinyl subscription, shipping exclusive pressings since 2022. Bluegrass reissues: Béla Fleck, Drive . J.D. Crowe & The New South (Rounder 0044). The Tony Rice Unit, Manzanita . Doc Watson. Plays: Nothing. He is a fan, and says so. On the show: Season 2, Episode 19
guests.heads: A group with one rule. "Send me money every month and I'll mail you a record". Pressing records for the people who made them. How a sellout led to Rounder. Working backward to John Hartford. Early on the Billy train
guests.text: If you have seen HWF on a t-shirt at a bluegrass show, you have met Kris Howland's work. A group with one rule Kris came out of the pandemic looking for company. He rejoined Facebook, joined a music group, and watched it fall apart. So he started his own, built around his own way of listening. The name began as a joke. Kris borrowed it from "Blood Sucking F(r)iends," a Greensky Bluegrass song by Dave Bruzza, where the "r" in parentheses lets you read it either way. Trevor admits he was in the group for a year before he noticed it was Fiends, not Friends. The founding rule is simple: no dunking on anyone's taste. Members post a record, name the artist and title, and talk about why they love it. Kris hits the love button even on records he would never play himself. "Nobody likes everything. Everybody loves someone. One of my buddies said that to me a few years back, and it sticks with me to this day." He hoped for 150 people to talk records with. It grew far past that. It mostly runs itself now, he says, and he still finds music there almost every day that he never knew existed. "If you can love something as much as I love my favorite things, we're solid. It doesn't matter about my feelings on it." "Send me money every month and I'll mail you a record" A member asked the group which record club he should join. Kris joked that he could send him money every month and get a record in the mail. About five weeks later, the club shipped 225 records to its first subscribers. Subscribers get one pressing a month. At first, Kris bought into runs that were already happening and added a signed card or an obi, the Japanese-style paper band that wraps the jacket. From the fourth release on, every record had to be exclusive to the club, either a color variant nobody else could sell or a pressing that existed only because the club made it. The club's catalog has since passed 50 releases. Fulfillment runs through Ridge Runner Records in Parkersburg, West Virginia, home of Kris's partner Erik Myers. Pressing records for the people who made them About half of the club's releases now are what Kris calls self-presses. He finds an artist who should be on vinyl but has no backing to get there. From mastering for vinyl to shipping, the club handles it. The first one Kris pressed himself was Kyle Tuttle's Labor of Lust , a record that was headed for CD and streaming only. The club got it mastered for vinyl, helped rework the artwork for the bigger format, and pressed it at Gotta Groove Records in Cleveland. Kyle got a stack of records for his merch table. Kris calls Kyle the mayor of progressive bluegrass in Nashville, and says doing right by him changed everything. Opportunities started coming to him through Kyle's friends. "We wanna be known as the most artist-focused label, record club, in the scene that we're all in together." How a sellout led to Rounder The bluegrass reissues started with a crash. Real Gone Music reissued John Hartford's Aereo-Plain , and a link to it landed in the group. It sold out in about half an hour. The label went looking for the source of the traffic and found a Facebook post by Kris. Gordon Anderson of Real Gone reached out. Kris, still new at this and plenty intimidated, pitched him the club. A few weeks later, Anderson came back with catalogs Kris could draw from, including Rounder, Vanguard and Flying Fish. Kris made a list on the spot. He picked records that shaped the bands he loves, and records that had become too rare and too expensive to find. Béla Fleck's Drive came first, in October 2023, its first vinyl pressing since the late 1980s. Next came J.D. Crowe & The New South , the record everyone knows as Rounder 0044, then Manzanita by the Tony Rice Unit and Doc Watson's self-titled 1964 debut on Vanguard. Rounder 0044 is personal. At Bender Jamboree in 2019, Jarrod Walker of Billy Strings's band told Kris he had to hear it before they could keep talking bluegrass. Walker wrote the set list and a note that night. It hangs in a shadow box at Kris's house. When the reissue came, Walker wrote new liner notes for it. Manzanita , pressed only once when it came out in 1979, became the club's most popular release. The goal, Kris says, is a clean, sealed copy of an essential record at a fair price, not $100 on the used market. Working backward to John Hartford Bluegrass was not something Kris heard growing up. He came to it through jam bands, Yonder Mountain String Band first, and then worked backward. He thought plenty of Hartford songs were Yonder originals before he knew better. Hartford, he says, is the trunk of his family tree on that side of his music. "A good band makes you listen to everything they've ever done. But a great band will make you listen to everything they've ever done and why they did everything that they did, all their influences." On the show, Kris broke the news of a club variant of Aereo-Plain in Cubs blue. He calls it a bit of an ego project, and a rite of passage. Early on the Billy train Kris and Trevor both caught Billy Strings early, back when you could buy a ticket at the door. The two still argue, mostly on Facebook, over whether the first pressing of Turmoil & Tinfoil came in anything other than pink. Kris stood on the arena floor in Denver not long before this conversation, watching a crowd bigger than all his early Billy venues put together. "The passion hasn't changed. The appreciation hasn't changed. It's just grown to more people."

guests.name: Michael Prewitt
guests.dek: Mandolin and songs, Michael Prewitt & CrunchGrass Supreme. Three years on the road with Special Consensus. A band name born outside a Taco Bell.
guests.bands: Michael Prewitt & CrunchGrass Supreme. Special Consensus. Back Up and Push
guests.glance: Plays: Mandolin, vocals, guitar. Home base: Williamsburg, Kentucky. Albums: The Peerless Mountain Sessions (2024). Something He Can Handle (2024). Recognition: Two IBMA Momentum Award nominations, Instrumentalist of the Year. Official showcase artist, IBMA Bluegrass Ramble, Chattanooga, 2025. On the show: Season 4, Episode 33
guests.heads: A bluegrass kid in southeastern Kentucky. The North Dakota detour. The call from Greg Cahill. Two records, back to back. CrunchGrass Supreme. Next up
guests.text: Michael Prewitt grew up on traditional bluegrass, took a long detour through graduate school in North Dakota, and came back to music by way of a voicemail from Greg Cahill. Now he leads a band named after a fast food order. A bluegrass kid in southeastern Kentucky Michael grew up in the Cumberland Mountain foothills of southeastern Kentucky. His dad was a big bluegrass fan, and the house ran on cassette tapes of J.D. Crowe and Flatt & Scruggs. His middle and high school had an after-school bluegrass band sponsored by the school district, and every year the band went to IBMA. He was a self-described little bluegrass nerd. He called in to Chris Jones's show on SiriusXM and once left a voicemail in his best Lester Flatt voice, a memory that still haunts him. He met Jones at IBMA and kept in touch for years. As a teenager he found the Grateful Dead and John Hartford online, and his taste ran from traditional toward the experimental. Old time came later, in his mid-twenties. The North Dakota detour Michael earned a degree in English literature. Late in his senior year, a professor asked if he had ever thought about grad school. He had not. Then the University of North Dakota sent him an invitation, and the far north had always pulled at him. He moved there two months later, earned his graduate degree, and taught at UND for a couple of years. He spent most of his twenties in North Dakota and Minnesota. He had mostly quit bluegrass by then. The problem, as he saw it, was that no middle ground seemed to exist. "Growing up, I didn't realize that there was anything in between somebody who jammed every Friday at the cabin and Ricky Skaggs. You could either be a superstar or you could jam." In his mid-twenties he found that middle ground in the Twin Cities, which has a strong bluegrass and roots scene. He played with a regional band, Back Up and Push, and started building a working life in music. The call from Greg Cahill Around 2018 or 2019, Chris Jones put Michael on the list of fill-in mandolin players for Special Consensus. COVID canceled the tour he was booked for. Then, in 2021, band leader Greg Cahill asked Jones for a mandolin player, and Jones gave him Michael's name. Michael did not pick up the unknown number. His phone transcribed the voicemail and spelled the name with a K. He thought it was a joke until he listened. It really was Greg Cahill, asking if he wanted the gig. Michael was working full time as a mail clerk and playing a lot of gigs on the side. "It didn't take me two seconds to be like, yes, I'd love this gig." He joined in the fall of 2021. For the next three years he toured with a band that, in his words, tours as much as anyone. Two records, back to back On a Special Consensus flight, Michael was listening to the Kentucky Colonels' live records. The sound was rough and the mics buzzed, and he loved it anyway. "Here I am, 50 years later, listening to it on an airplane, and loving it. This is exactly what I needed to be hearing at this moment." That became The Peerless Mountain Sessions : a trio record of mandolin, banjo and bass, with no guitar, to leave room in the middle. Brady Wallen, a friend since high school, played banjo. Dan Eubanks, his Special Consensus bandmate, played bass. They cut it live in one day with few microphones and next to no arranging. The tunes ranged from Métis fiddle tunes to old-time Kentucky tunes and Bill Monroe. It came out in 2024 on Common Loon Records, a small label out of Dothan, Alabama. His take on "Tombstone Junction" is still his most-streamed track. That record did better than he expected, and it gave him the confidence for a bigger one. Something He Can Handle , a full-band album of mostly original songs, followed in the fall of 2024 and has earned steady SiriusXM play. CrunchGrass Supreme Michael left Special Consensus at the end of 2024, after giving a year's notice. He wanted a break from the road and more control over when, where and how he works. He moved back to Kentucky, where he teaches English online at the university in Williamsburg. The band name goes back a few years earlier. After a pickup gig at a bluegrass bar on Lower Broadway in Nashville, Michael walked past the Taco Bell on Broadway, which has its own stage and drum kit. He announced that his life goal was to play there. He would need a band for that, and a name. "CrunchGrass Supreme" came out on the spot, and he told his friends not to steal it. When dates started coming in for 2025, he never came up with anything better. "It's not maybe the best thing in the world, but at 2:00 AM sometimes it's as good as you can get." The band was an official showcase artist at IBMA in Chattanooga in 2025. At a late-night showcase that same week, he ate a Crunchwrap Supreme on stage in the middle of a song. There is video. Next up Next is his first album of all original songs, recorded by the band itself with no session players, with a fall 2026 release in view. His website lists the new collection as Poor Ol' Pitiful Human . The band has festival dates from Colorado to Missouri to Alberta to North Dakota. Michael also plays solo shows, house concerts and duo shows with bandmate Aaron Bibelhauser, and planned a three-week solo tour of England. "I'm never happier than when I'm playing music and on the road." Off stage, he collects vintage trucker hats, including a 1987 Minnesota Twins World Series cap. The Cincinnati Reds are his National League team. He also collects vinyl, CDs and cassettes, and is working through the whole Flying Fish Records catalog in order of release. Lately that means Buddy Emmons' Steel Guitar .

guests.name: Randy Steele
guests.dek: Banjo player, songwriter and bandleader of Randy Steele and the High Cold Wind. Retired Chattanooga firefighter. A friend of the show.
guests.bands: Randy Steele and the High Cold Wind. Slim Pickins Bluegrass Band
guests.glance: Plays: Banjo and vocals. Guitar and bass too. Home base: Chattanooga, Tennessee. Grew up in Bradley County. Records: Songs from the Suck (2016). Moccasin Bender EP (2018). High Cold Wind EP (2023). Singles with producer Nick Lutsko. Songwriting: Independent Music Award, Bluegrass Song of the Year, 2018, for "Mobile Soon." Kerrville New Folk finalist, 2023. Telluride: Second place, Telluride Band Contest, 2026, with the High Cold Wind. On the show: Season 3, Episodes 25, 26 and 28
guests.heads: A record player and a jam band. The banjo pulls him back. Slim Pickins and the road. Songs from the Suck. The High Cold Wind. Bluegrass church on Tuesdays. Bringing the World of Bluegrass home
guests.text: Randy is a friend of the show and its most frequent co-host. A record player and a jam band "Spoon River Breakdown" Randy Steele and The High Cold Wind June 23, 2026 0:27 Randy grew up in Bradley County, Tennessee. His grandfather loved bluegrass but could not play it. What he had was a double live album from Bean Blossom, Bill Monroe's festival, with the Osborne Brothers, Jim and Jesse and the rest of the old guard. Randy listened to it with him over and over. His own path ran through the Grateful Dead, Phish and the Allman Brothers. He played electric guitar in a regional jam band and studied studio music and jazz guitar at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville. Then he took an EMT license, went to work on an ambulance, and joined the Chattanooga Fire Department. For a few years music took a back seat. The banjo pulls him back O Brother, Where Art Thou? sent him back to bluegrass. A friend put a banjo in his hands, he found a good teacher, and he fell hard. He started on fiddle first, and he recommends it as a strategy. "Nothing is as annoying as learning how to play the fiddle, I promise you." After a year or two on the banjo, he saw Noam Pikelny play a trio show with David Grier and Shad Cobb at Barking Legs Theater in Chattanooga. It changed what he thought the instrument could do. Trevor was in the room that night too. So were the future members of Slim Pickins, none of whom knew each other yet. "Bluegrass banjo is what pulled me back into playing music. Ever since then, I've really been attached to it." Slim Pickins and the road His first bluegrass band was a weeknight picking circle with friends. When he wanted to play with stronger players, he answered a Craigslist ad for a banjo player and joined Slim Pickins. The band started playing out in 2008 and opened for the Infamous Stringdusters early on. In 2016 Slim Pickins toured Europe for about a month, playing Belgium and Holland and something like 31 shows in 28 days. The trip showed Randy how much he wanted to play live. It also formed the core of a new band. For the first half of the tour they ran as a four piece, with Randy, mandolinist John Boulware , bassist Justin Hupp and a young picker named Tyler Martelli. Songs from the Suck Slim Pickins "Cannonballs" November 15, 2025 2:17 Randy wrote most of Slim Pickins' songs, and the Europe trip pushed him to make a solo record. He cut much of Songs from the Suck at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals and finished it near Soddy-Daisy. The title points to Suck Creek, which meets the Tennessee River just upstream of Chattanooga. Before the TVA dams, the rapids there, known as the Suck, were among the most feared stretches of the river. One song, "Mobile Soon," won the 2018 Independent Music Award for Bluegrass Song of the Year and took Randy to the ceremony at Lincoln Center in New York. The 2018 EP Moccasin Bender followed, and its song "Age of Ben" made the semifinals of American Songwriter's song contest. In 2019 he played 134 solo shows across more than 20 states while still working full time at the fire department. In 2023 he was one of 24 finalists in the Kerrville New Folk competition for emerging songwriters. The High Cold Wind After the pandemic, Randy wanted to play as much bluegrass as he could. The High Cold Wind started as the band on a record and became a working unit in 2022. Most of its members came out of Slim Pickins. The lineup now is Randy on banjo and vocals, Brad Clark on guitar, John Boulware on mandolin and Justin Hupp on bass. Lately the band has worked on opening up its jams. Randy learned to improvise in jam bands and jazz school before bluegrass, and he has pushed the band to stretch and listen harder, even running drills at practice. In March 2025 he released "The Extra Mile Is a Gravel Road," produced by Nick Lutsko. "It's about having a good time, and as long as we keep it about having a good time, I think we're in good shape." In June 2026 the band drove 1,600 miles to the Telluride Band Contest in Colorado. They made the final four, played the main stage, and finished second to the Litch Brothers of Orcas Island, Washington. Bluegrass church on Tuesdays Randy hosts a free jam every Tuesday at Barrelhouse Ballroom in downtown Chattanooga. It opens with a slow jam for beginners. He posts an eight-song set list a week ahead, mostly songs in G, C and D, so newcomers can practice. After that the floor opens to anyone. It grew fast. "We try to introduce ourselves to every person that comes in the door and treat it like a bluegrass church." Festival campground jams hooked Randy as a young player. The Tuesday jam puts that experience in public, where anyone can find it. Bringing the World of Bluegrass home When IBMA announced it would leave Raleigh, Randy sent an email to the right people in Chattanooga. He is quick to hand the credit to Visit Chattanooga, who took the idea and ran with it. WMOT later described him as the only musician on the local organizing committee that worked with IBMA. When IBMA leaders came to look at the city in late 2023, Randy made sure there was a pop-up bluegrass band waiting for them at dinner. IBMA's executive director at the time, Ken White , was one of the visitors. World of Bluegrass came to Chattanooga in September 2025. That week the High Cold Wind played Noontunes downtown and two official showcases on the Bluegrass Ramble, their first. Randy retired from the fire department as a captain earlier that year. Before the festival, Randy co-hosted two episodes with Trevor, walking through the Ramble and main stage lineups. Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.

guests.heads: IBMA from the inside. Joining Wood Box Heroes. The Never-Ending Years. What came next
guests.text: Thomas Cassell was Trevor's first interview, back in season one. In September 2025 he came back for the show's first bonus episode, recorded ten days before IBMA came to Chattanooga. IBMA from the inside Thomas Cassell "New November" December 18, 2024 3:02 Thomas has worked IBMA's World of Bluegrass every year since 2016, including the virtual year. Some years he played 15 to 20 showcases in a week, walking from room to room with his mandolin out of the case. He also served on the education committee that sorted panel proposals and built the conference schedule. His favorite part of the business side is the Momentum Awards luncheon, where he gets to sit with friends and watch them win. The panel that changed the most for him was a 2019 session on social media. He came home and rebuilt how Circus No. 9 handled its accounts. Five months later the pandemic changed the whole internet, and he started over. "For three or four hours a day, I'm a professional. And for the other ten or so hours, I'm just totally a fan at IBMA." He likes the week for the same reason everyone does. At a festival you might see a friend for an hour. At IBMA the whole industry is in one place for days. "It's the big old family reunion, almost." When IBMA announced it was leaving Raleigh, Thomas guessed the next stop would be Knoxville or Chattanooga. He was glad to be right. Joining Wood Box Heroes Thomas joined Wood Box Heroes on mandolin in 2024, taking over from founding member Seth Taylor. The band is Josh Martin on guitar and lead vocals, Matt Menefee on banjo, Jenee Fleenor on fiddle and Barry Bales on bass. For a young band, the Grand Ole Opry came early. By the end of August 2025, Thomas had played the Opry four times with them. On the fourth, Vince Gill sat in for a song. IBMA took longer. A ramble slot opened late in the summer of 2025, and the band played its first World of Bluegrass in Chattanooga. "I have to pinch myself constantly being in there." Matt Menefee and Barry Bales were the players he watched on YouTube as a teenager. Josh Martin and Jenee Fleenor he calls two of the best musicians and front people he has ever played with. The Never-Ending Years Circus No. 9 "Chesapeake" February 9, 2019 2:05. Circus No. 9, the band Thomas founded His third solo album, The Never-Ending Years , came out on Mountain Fever Records in October 2024. He co-produced it with Casey Campbell. Thomas made a lot of phone calls for this one. There are two core bands. One is his own generation, with Jake Stargel, Cory Walker and Jason Carter. The other is what he calls his hero band: Ron Stewart on banjo, Tim Stafford on guitar and Bronwyn Keith-Hynes on fiddle. Rob Ickes, Bob Minner and Wyatt Rice sit in. The singers include Dale Ann Bradley and Missy Raines, and Ronnie McCoury sings two duets with him. Thomas was after the sound of Ronnie and Del McCoury singing together, one of his favorite things in the world. The CD comes with full liner notes: lyrics and who wrote each song. His website lists full credits for every record he has made. "When I get a record, I'm like, man, I wanna know everything about everything that's on this." What came next After IBMA 2025, Thomas played a mandolin and guitar duo set and emceed the Mayhaw Music Festival in Cottonwood, Alabama, his first time as an emcee. Then came a run of October festivals with Wood Box Heroes, including a stop in his hometown of Big Stone Gap. He told Trevor he had a solo project in the works, with duets alongside guitar players. It came out in 2026 on Common Loon Records as Guitar Collection . Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.
